top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) is a mature, experimentally reproduced measurement advance: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms removes Doppler, recoil and trap shifts and beats the quantum-projection-noise limit of single-ion clocks, with independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) agreeing at the 1e-18 level. It is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, and it is the only slate proposal with a clean two-name allocation that every discussing member reached. The citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice, not the accuracy figure or the future redefinition of the second. IceCube diffuse flux ranks second because it is a real discovery but the Halzen-Karle credit is unresolved; the topological insulator trio ranks third because of the omitted Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang contributions and the 2016 prize overlap, though all three are preferred to no award.
recusal_note: Mild: a PhD-year stay in John Hall's laboratory, whose laser-stabilisation and comb work underlies the clock field and is linked to Jun Ye's group at JILA, but no collaboration or supervision with Katori or Ye; Lund and WACQT quantum-information ties are not relevant to these proposals. Not recusal-level.
